1.q: מַשָּׂ֖א בָּבֶ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר חָזָ֔ה יְשַׁעְיָ֖הוּ בֶּן־אָמֽוֹץ
1.note: The title is speaking of this message about Babylon as if it were a burden, that is, a heavy load to carry. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The message about Babylon that Isaiah, the son of Amoz, received]
The name of the city stands for the people of Babylon. Alternate translation: [the people of Babylon]
Amoz was the father of Isaiah. See how you translated this in [Isaiah 1:1](ta:01).

2.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the Mede and Persian warriors whom Yahweh is summoning to battle. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to Yahweh’s warriors]

Here, **that** marks **they may enter the gates of the nobles** as the goal or purpose of lifting up a banner, raising a voice, and waving a hand. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [informing them that they should enter]

3.note: Yahweh is repeating the pronoun **I** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, have commanded]

Yahweh is using **for my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of my anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of my anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my proud glory]

4.note: Isaiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, alarm at the noise of armies gathering. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what made him alarmed. Alternate translation: [Oh, the sound of a multitude in the mountains]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a numerous people** produces a great noise, so does the multitude in the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like the roar that a great crowd would make]

The expression **nations being gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [nations that Yahweh is gathering]

Isaiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, alarm, at the commotion of kingdoms assembling for war. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what made him alarmed. Alternate translation: [What an alarming commotion of kingdoms, nations that Yahweh is gathering]

5.note: These two phrases **from a land of distance** and **from the end of the heavens** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [from a very distant land]

Isaiah is speaking of the soldiers whom Yahweh is sending as if they were **the weapons of his indignation**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the soldiers he is sending in his anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **indignation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his anger]

Here, **to** marks **destroy all of the land** as the goal or purpose of Yahweh and the weapons of his indignation coming from distant lands. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that they can destroy]

Isaiah says **all of the land** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the entire land]

6.q: קָר֖וֹב י֣וֹם יְהוָ֑ה כְּ⁠שֹׁ֖ד מִ⁠שַּׁדַּ֥י יָבֽוֹא
6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **destruction from Shaddai** is sudden and devastating, so is the coming of the **day of Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the day of Yahweh will come suddenly and devastatingly, just as destruction from Shaddai comes]

This is poetic language. In the original language, the words translated as **destruction** and **Shaddai** sound similar to each other, creating a wordplay. If your language has a way to express this effect, you could use it here.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like a destroying blow]

7.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]

Isaiah says **all of the hands** and **every heart** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [everyone’s hands will drop and everyone’s heart will melt]

Here, **all of the hands will drop** represents the people losing their strength and courage. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the people will lose their strength and courage]

The masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and every heart of every person]

Isaiah is speaking of the people’s courage, their **heart**, as if it were a solid object that could **melt**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and everyone’s courage will fail]

8.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Babylonians. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Babylonians will be terrified]

The expression **they will be terrified** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And terror will seize them]

Isaiah is speaking of **pangs and agonies** as if they were living things that could **seize** people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will suffer pangs and agonies]

The terms **pangs** and **agonies** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [intense pain]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one birthing** writhes in great pain, so will the Babylonians writhe in their agony. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as a woman writhes in great pain when she gives birth, so they will writhe in agony]

The masculine terms **A man** and **his friend** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [A person will marvel to a neighbor]

Isaiah is speaking of the people’s faces as if they were **faces of flames**, meaning their faces will be flushed with distress. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their faces will be flushed with distress]

9.note: Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Isaiah is speaking of **the day of Yahweh** as if it were a living thing that could be **cruel** and come on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will come and be cruel]

Isaiah is using **burning of nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “fierce anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and fierce anger]

The terms **wrath** and **burning of nose** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with great wrath]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wrath** and **desolation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [a completely ruined place]

10.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of what will happen. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what came before it. Alternate translation: [And]

11.note: Yahweh begins speaking here without an explicit introduction in the text. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh said,]

Yahweh is using **I will visit upon the world its evil** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will bring judgment on the world for its evil.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will bring judgment on the world for its evil]

Yahweh is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

11.q: וְ⁠הִשְׁבַּתִּי֙ גְּא֣וֹן זֵדִ֔ים וְ⁠גַאֲוַ֥ת עָרִיצִ֖ים אַשְׁפִּֽיל
11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will make the boasting of the arrogant cease, and I will bring low the haughtiness of the mighty]

Yahweh is using the adjective **arrogant** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are arrogant]

Yahweh is using the adjective **mighty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [mighty people]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **iniquity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [wicked deeds, and upon the wicked, their moral corruption]

12.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **fine gold** is rare and precious, so will **a man** become rare after Yahweh’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [After my judgment, a man will be more rare than fine gold]

12.q: אוֹקִ֥יר אֱנ֖וֹשׁ מִ⁠פָּ֑ז וְ⁠אָדָ֖ם מִ⁠כֶּ֥תֶם אוֹפִֽיר
12.note: Yahweh says **I will make a man rarer than fine gold** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I will make it so that people are extremely scarce, yes, it will be hard to find people]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and a human I will make rarer than the pure gold of Ophir]

12.q: אוֹקִ֥יר אֱנ֖וֹשׁ מִ⁠פָּ֑ז וְ⁠אָדָ֖ם מִ⁠כֶּ֥תֶם אוֹפִֽיר
12.note: The masculine terms **a man** and **a human** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [I will make a person rarer than fine gold, and a human being I will make rarer than the pure gold of Ophir.]

13.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [This is why]

Yahweh is speaking of **the heavens** and **the earth** as if they were living things that could **tremble** and **shake** with fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will cause the heavens to shake, and the earth will move from its place]

Yahweh is referring to all of creation by naming two major components, **the heavens** and **the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will make everything tremble and shake from its place]

13.q: בְּ⁠עֶבְרַת֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת וּ⁠בְ⁠י֖וֹם חֲר֥וֹן אַפּֽ⁠וֹ
13.note: Even though Yahweh is the one speaking, he is referring to himself in the third person as **Yahweh of Armies** and using the pronoun **his** to speak of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [at my wrath and in the day of the burning of my nose]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because Yahweh of Armies is enraged]

Yahweh is using **the burning of his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “his fierce anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his fierce anger]

14.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the situation in Babylon after Yahweh’s judgment. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the situation in Babylon will be]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a chased gazelle** flees in terror, so will the people in Babylon flee. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a gazelle fleeing in terror from hunters]

The expression **a chased gazelle** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a gazelle that hunters are chasing]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a flock with no gatherer** scatters without direction, so will the people in Babylon scatter in confusion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [or like a flock of sheep that scatters when there is no one to herd them together]

14.q: אִ֤ישׁ אֶל־עַמּ⁠וֹ֙ יִפְנ֔וּ וְ⁠אִ֥ישׁ אֶל־אַרְצ֖⁠וֹ יָנֽוּסוּ
14.note: Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person will turn to their people and each person will flee to their land]

15.note: The expression **Every one found will be stabbed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The enemy will stab everyone they find]

The expression **every one swept up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and every one they catch]

Here, **the sword** represents warfare and violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will fall in battle]

Isaiah says **Every one found** and **every one swept up** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Whoever is found will be stabbed, and whoever is swept up will fall by the sword]

16.q: וְ⁠עֹלְלֵי⁠הֶ֥ם יְרֻטְּשׁ֖וּ לְ⁠עֵֽינֵי⁠הֶ֑ם יִשַּׁ֨סּוּ֙ בָּֽתֵּי⁠הֶ֔ם וּ⁠נְשֵׁי⁠הֶ֖ם תשגלנה
16.note: The expressions **their infants will be dashed**, **their houses will be plundered**, and **their wives will be ravished** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And their enemies will dash their infants before their eyes; they will plunder their houses, and they will ravish their wives]

Isaiah is using **to their eyes** to represent the parents seeing what happens. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before their eyes]

Isaiah is referring to sexual assault in a polite way by using the phrase **will be ravished**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and their wives will be raped]

17.note: Yahweh begins speaking again here without an explicit introduction in the text. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language, as modeled by the UST.

Yahweh is using **Behold me, awakening** as a common expression of the culture to mean “pay attention, I am about to stir up.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention! I am about to stir up]

18.note: Yahweh is using **bows** to represent the archers who use them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The archers will dash young men]

Yahweh is using **the fruit of the womb** as a common expression of the culture to mean “children” or “babies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the children]

18.q: וּ⁠פְרִי־בֶ֨טֶן֙ לֹ֣א יְרַחֵ֔מוּ עַל־בָּנִ֖ים לֹֽא־תָח֥וּס עֵינָֽ⁠ם
18.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **compassion** and **pity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and they will not have tender concern; their eye will not have sympathy on sons]

Yahweh is using **their eye** to represent the Medes themselves and their emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they themselves will not have pity on sons]

19.q: וְ⁠הָיְתָ֤ה בָבֶל֙ צְבִ֣י מַמְלָכ֔וֹת תִּפְאֶ֖רֶת גְּא֣וֹן כַּשְׂדִּ֑ים כְּ⁠מַהְפֵּכַ֣ת אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֶת־סְדֹ֖ם וְ⁠אֶת־עֲמֹרָֽה
19.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the destruction of God** of Sodom and Gomorrah was complete and permanent, so will be the destruction of Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And Babylon, the glory of the kingdoms, the splendor of the pride of the Chaldeans, will be utterly destroyed, just as God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah]

The terms **glory** and **splendor** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the most magnificent kingdom, about which the Chaldeans boasted]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory**, **splendor**, and **pride**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [most glorious of the kingdoms, the most magnificent of what the Chaldeans held dear]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like what God did to the cities]

20.q: לֹֽא־תֵשֵׁ֣ב לָ⁠נֶ֔צַח וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִשְׁכֹּ֖ן עַד־דּ֣וֹר וָ⁠ד֑וֹר
20.note: Isaiah says **It will not dwell, to eternity** and **one will not inhabit, to generation and generation** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [No one will ever live there again, and in all future generations no one will settle there]

20.q: לֹֽא־תֵשֵׁ֣ב לָ⁠נֶ֔צַח וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִשְׁכֹּ֖ן עַד־דּ֣וֹר וָ⁠ד֑וֹר
20.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [It will not be home to anyone ever again]

Isaiah assumes that readers will know it is sheep which **shepherds will not make lie down there**. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and shepherds will not make their sheep lie down there]

21.note: The pronoun **their** refers to the former inhabitants of Babylon, not to the desert creatures. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the houses of the people who once lived there]

Isaiah is using **daughters of the ostrich** as a common expression of the culture to mean “ostriches.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ostriches]

22.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and jackals will cry out in palaces of luxury]

Isaiah is speaking of Babylon’s **time** of judgment as if it were a living thing that could **come** on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And its destruction will happen soon]

The expression **its days will not be prolonged** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and its days will not last long]

Here, **its days** represents Babylon’s remaining time as a city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the time Babylon has left]
